title: CUET Mass Media Test 2
subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Mass Media - 318.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Mass Media papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: CBSE Mass Media Studies, Classes XI-XII (curriculum mirrored by the NTA syllabus)
Constitution of India, Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(2); Acts and Supreme Court judgments as cited
Official histories of All India Radio, Doordarshan and Indian cinema
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a case; the set stays together.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.sub_topic: The web in which users create content
questions.question: The stage of the internet in which users create and share content, rather than only read it, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Web 2.0
Why: Web 2.0 is the interactive web of blogs, social media and wikis, where users create content.
Why not the others: (A) was the earlier, read-only web. (B) is a hidden part of the internet. (C) is a private network inside an organisation.
Key point: Web 2.0 turned the audience into producers.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: Stages of making a film
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the stages of film-making:
(A) Pre-production includes writing the script, casting and finding locations.
(B) Dubbing is done during the production (shooting) stage.
(C) In distribution, the film is supplied to cinema halls and other outlets.
(D) Exhibition means screening the film to the public.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false. Dubbing, like editing and mixing, is done in post-production, after the shooting is over.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are correct. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: The stages run pre-production, production, post-production, distribution and exhibition.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: Television programme formats
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Format)
(A) Reality show
(B) Docudrama
(C) Game show
(D) Talk show

List-II (Feature)
(I) Ordinary people are filmed in unscripted situations
(II) A host discusses a topic with invited guests
(III) Actors re-create real events
(IV) Contestants compete for prizes
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: A reality show films people in unscripted situations (I). A docudrama dramatises real events (III). In a game show contestants compete for prizes (IV), and in a talk show a host talks to guests (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps reality show and docudrama. (B) swaps docudrama and game show. (C) swaps game show and talk show.
Key point: Each format has its own structure and audience appeal.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.sub_topic: Good manners online
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about netiquette:
(A) Typing a whole message in capital letters is read as shouting.
(B) One should identify oneself when writing to people one does not know.
(C) It is fine to forward an unverified message if it comes from a friend.
(D) One should not post other people's photos without their consent.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Capitals look like shouting, a writer should say who they are, and others' privacy must be respected.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Forwarding unverified messages spreads rumours and fake news, whoever sent them. Options (B) and (C) include (C), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Netiquette is about respect, honesty and responsibility online.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: The state body that funded parallel films
questions.question: Which government body, into which the Film Finance Corporation was merged, gave loans and support to many parallel cinema films?
options: B) Central Board of Film Certification
C) Film and Television Institute of India
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) National Film Development Corporation
Why: The NFDC (1975) took over the Film Finance Corporation in 1980 and funded many low-budget films by new directors.
Why not the others: (B) certifies films for screening. (C) trains film-makers. (D) organises film festivals.
Key point: State funding helped parallel cinema survive outside the box office.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Using another writer's work as one's own
questions.question: A reporter copies whole paragraphs from another journalist's article into her own story without giving credit. This is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Plagiarism
Why: Plagiarism means presenting someone else's words or ideas as one's own without credit.
Why not the others: (B) damages a person's reputation with false statements. (C) exaggerates news to excite the reader. (D) disrespects a court or interferes with justice.
Key point: Journalists must credit the sources of material they use.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.sub_topic: Hearing only views one already holds
questions.question: When a social media user sees only posts that repeat views they already hold, the effect is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) An echo chamber
Why: In an echo chamber, algorithms and choice of contacts mean a person hears only views like their own, so opinions harden.
Why not the others: (B) is the gap between those who have internet access and those who do not. (C) is McLuhan's idea of a world linked by media. (D) is the ability to judge media content.
Key point: Echo chambers are one of the socio-political risks of new media.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: The director's link on the studio floor
questions.question: The person who passes on the director's instructions to the presenters and crew in the studio is the ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) floor manager
Why: The floor manager is the director's link on the studio floor. They cue presenters, give time signals and keep the floor running.
Why not the others: (A) operates a camera. (B) switches between camera feeds in the control room. (C) writes the script before production.
Key point: The director sits in the control room, so the floor manager speaks for them in the studio.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: What is not non-verbal communication
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a form of non-verbal communication?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A written letter
Why: A written letter uses words, so it is verbal communication even though it is not spoken.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) send messages without words, through the face, touch and the body.
Key point: Verbal communication may be spoken or written; non-verbal communication uses no words.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: The model that added the gatekeeper
questions.question: Which model of communication added the role of the gatekeeper, such as an editor who selects which messages reach the audience?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Westley and MacLean's model
Why: Westley and MacLean's model (1957) was built for mass communication. It added a gatekeeper (C) who selects and shapes messages before they reach the audience.
Why not the others: (A) lists source, message, channel and receiver. (B) is a verbal formula of five questions. (C) is a technical model that adds noise.
Key point: In the mass media, editors and producers act as gatekeepers.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Landmark judgments on freedom of the press
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about court judgments:
(A) In Romesh Thappar (1950), the Supreme Court held that freedom of the press is part of freedom of speech and expression.
(B) In Bennett Coleman (1972), the Supreme Court upheld the government's control over the number of pages a newspaper could print.
(C) In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act.
(D) In K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), the Supreme Court held that privacy is a fundamental right.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A), (C) and (D) are correct. Romesh Thappar placed press freedom within Article 19(1)(a). Shreya Singhal struck down Section 66A, which punished "offensive" online posts. Puttaswamy declared privacy a fundamental right.
Why not the others: (B) is false. In Bennett Coleman the Court struck down the newsprint policy that limited pages, holding that it violated press freedom. Options (B) and (D) include (B), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: The courts have read press freedom into Article 19(1)(a).

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: How the producer speaks to the presenter
questions.question: The system that lets a producer in the control room speak to a presenter through earphones without going on air is called ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) talkback
Why: Talkback is a private link from the control room to the studio. The listeners do not hear it.
Why not the others: (A) is the howl when a microphone picks up its own speaker, or the response of an audience. (B) is replaying recorded sound. (C) is lowering sound to silence.
Key point: Talkback lets the producer guide a live programme.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Parts of a newspaper page and story
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Byline
(B) Dateline
(C) Deck
(D) Masthead

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A smaller headline set below the main headline
(II) The newspaper's name and logo at the top of the front page
(III) The place and date from which a story is filed
(IV) The line giving the writer's name
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: The byline names the writer (IV) and the dateline gives the place and date of filing (III). The deck is a secondary headline below the main one (I), and the masthead is the paper's name at the top of page one (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps byline and dateline. (C) swaps deck and masthead. (D) swaps dateline and deck.
Key point: Each part of a news page has a fixed name and job.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: What TRP stands for
questions.question: In television, TRP stands for:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Television Rating Point
Why: TRP (Television Rating Point) measures what share of the target audience watched a programme.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not the terms used.
Key point: Ratings decide advertising rates and which programmes stay on air.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: What a journalist should not be
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a quality of a good journalist?
options: D) A good command of language
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Siding with one party
Why: Siding with one party leads to partisan reporting, which goes against the fairness a journalist must keep.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are all qualities a journalist needs.
Key point: A journalist should be fair and balanced, presenting all sides.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: Visiting a location before the shoot
questions.question: Before a shoot, the director and the camera team visit the location to check light, space, sound and permissions. This visit is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Recce
Why: A recce (short for reconnaissance) is a survey of a location before shooting, to plan the cameras, lights and sound.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are practice runs with the actors or presenters. (C) is a first assembly of the edited footage.
Key point: The recce is part of pre-production.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Barriers to communication
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Barrier)
(A) Semantic barrier
(B) Physical barrier
(C) Psychological barrier
(D) Cultural barrier

List-II (Example)
(I) A worried listener who has already decided the speaker is wrong
(II) A word that means one thing to the speaker and another to the listener
(III) A thumbs-up that is friendly in one country and rude in another
(IV) Traffic noise drowning out a speech at a street corner
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: A semantic barrier comes from the meaning of words (II). A physical barrier comes from the surroundings, such as noise (IV). A psychological barrier lies in the mind, such as prejudice or worry (I). A cultural barrier arises when signs mean different things in different cultures (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps physical and psychological. (B) swaps semantic and cultural. (D) swaps psychological and cultural.
Key point: Barriers can lie in language, surroundings, the mind or culture.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.sub_topic: Online movements and their causes
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Movement)
(A) #MeToo
(B) India Against Corruption (2011)
(C) Arab Spring (2010–11)
(D) Nirbhaya protests (2012)
List-II (Cause)
(I) A demand for a Jan Lokpal law
(II) Uprisings against governments in West Asia and North Africa
(III) Safety of women after a gang rape in Delhi
(IV) Speaking out against sexual harassment
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: #MeToo let people speak out about sexual harassment (IV). India Against Corruption demanded a Jan Lokpal (I). The Arab Spring was a wave of uprisings (II), and the Nirbhaya protests demanded safety for women (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps India Against Corruption and the Arab Spring. (C) swaps #MeToo and Nirbhaya. (D) swaps the Arab Spring and Nirbhaya.
Key point: Social media helped each movement gather people quickly.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.sub_topic: Emerging trends in new media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about trends in new media:
(A) OTT platforms stream films and shows directly over the internet.
(B) Podcasts are audio programmes that listeners can play on demand.
(C) Mobile journalism means reporting, shooting and editing stories on a smartphone.
(D) Data journalism avoids numbers and relies on opinion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. OTT ("over the top") services bypass cable and broadcast. Podcasts are on-demand audio. Mobile journalism uses a phone for the whole story.
Why not the others: (D) is false. Data journalism finds and tells stories by analysing data. Options (B) and (D) include (D), and (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: New media is changing how content is made and consumed.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.sub_topic: India's main law on cyber crime
questions.question: Which law is India's main law dealing with cyber crime and electronic records?
options: A) Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Information Technology Act, 2000
Why: The Information Technology Act, 2000 deals with electronic records, digital signatures and offences such as hacking and identity theft.
Why not the others: (A) governs the registration of newspapers and books. (C) governs telegraph and telephone lines. (D) concerns films.
Key point: The IT Act is the legal base for fighting cyber crime.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: Who certifies films for screening
questions.question: Films in India must be certified before they are screened in public. This is done by the:
options: A) Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
C) Central Board of Film Certification
D) National Film Archive of India
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Central Board of Film Certification
Why: The CBFC certifies films under the Cinematograph Act, 1952, in categories such as U, UA and A.
Why not the others: (A) is the ministry under which the CBFC works, but it does not certify films itself. (B) produces documentaries for the government. (D) preserves old films.
Key point: Film certification is a legal restriction on public exhibition.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: A poor habit in a radio script
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT good practice when writing a radio script?
options: A) Repeating the main point near the end
B) Reading out figures in full, like 3,47,862
C) Using short and simple sentences
D) Writing in a conversational tone
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Reading out figures in full, like 3,47,862
Why: A listener cannot go back and re-read, so exact figures are hard to follow. Radio writers round them off, for example "about three and a half lakh".
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) all help a listener follow by ear.
Key point: Radio is written for the ear, not the eye.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Models of communication in order of time
questions.question:
Arrange the following models of communication in the order in which they were put forward:
(A) Berlo's SMCR model
(B) Aristotle's model of speaker, speech and audience
(C) Osgood and Schramm's circular model
(D) Lasswell's model
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (C), (A)
Why: Aristotle's model of rhetoric dates from ancient Greece. Lasswell's model came in 1948, Osgood and Schramm's circular model in 1954, and Berlo's SMCR model in 1960.
Why not the others: (A) puts the 1954 model before 1948. (C) puts Lasswell before Aristotle. (D) puts Berlo (1960) before Osgood and Schramm (1954).
Key point: Models moved from one-way (linear) to two-way (circular) over time.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: Shot sizes from widest to closest
questions.question:
Arrange the following camera shots from the widest to the closest:
(A) Medium shot
(B) Close-up
(C) Extreme long shot
(D) Long shot
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: An extreme long shot shows a vast area, and a long shot shows the whole figure in its setting. A medium shot shows a person from the waist up, and a close-up fills the frame with a face.
Why not the others: (A) puts the long shot before the extreme long shot. (B) puts the medium shot before the long shot. (D) puts the close-up before the medium shot.
Key point: Shot size controls how much the viewer sees and how close they feel.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.sub_topic: One company spread across many media
questions.question: When one media company owns a newspaper, a TV channel, a radio station and a news website, this is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Economic convergence
Why: Economic convergence is the joining of different media under one owner, so that content and costs can be shared.
Why not the others: (A) is one device doing many jobs, such as a smartphone. (C) is the blending of cultures through media. (D) is reporting by ordinary people.
Key point: Convergence has technical, economic and cultural sides.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: The law that protects state secrets
questions.question: Which law makes it an offence to publish information that may harm the security of the state?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Official Secrets Act, 1923
Why: The Official Secrets Act, 1923 punishes spying and the disclosure of secret government information that may harm national security.
Why not the others: (A) set up the Press Council to keep up press standards. (B) gives citizens a right to information. (C) protects creative works.
Key point: The Act is one of the reasonable restrictions on press freedom.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Public campaigns and their causes
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Campaign)
(A) Jago Grahak Jago
(B) Incredible India
(C) Pulse Polio
(D) Swachh Bharat

List-II (Cause)
(I) Promoting India as a tourist destination
(II) Cleanliness and sanitation
(III) Making buyers aware of their rights
(IV) Immunising children, with the slogan "Do boond zindagi ki"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Jago Grahak Jago, run by the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, tells buyers about their rights (III). Incredible India promotes tourism (I). Pulse Polio immunises children against polio (IV), and Swachh Bharat is about cleanliness (II).
Why not the others: (B) swaps Jago Grahak Jago and Incredible India. (C) swaps Pulse Polio and Swachh Bharat. (D) swaps Incredible India and Pulse Polio.
Key point: Governments use advertising campaigns for social causes, not only for selling products.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: How copy moves through a newsroom
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps in the order in which a news story moves through a newspaper:
(A) The news editor decides where the story goes on the page.
(B) The press prints the edition.
(C) The reporter gathers the facts and files the copy.
(D) The sub-editor checks the copy, trims it and writes the headline.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: The reporter first gathers the facts and files the story. The sub-editor then checks, edits and headlines it. The news editor places it on the page, and the press prints the edition last.
Why not the others: (B) places the story before it is edited. (C) edits copy that has not yet been filed. (D) prints before the page is planned.
Key point: A story passes through several gatekeepers before it is printed.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Advertising a banned product through a namesake
questions.question: A liquor company that may not advertise its whisky runs advertisements for "music CDs" and "soda" sold under the same brand name. This is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Surrogate advertising
Why: In surrogate advertising, a brand whose main product cannot be advertised promotes another item with the same name, so that the brand stays in public view.
Why not the others: (A) compares one brand with another. (C) is shared between two advertisers. (D) promotes a company's image.
Key point: Surrogate advertising is a way around a ban, and Indian rules try to stop it.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: Radio programme formats
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Format)
(A) Phone-in
(B) Radio feature
(C) Radio drama
(D) Radio talk

List-II (Feature)
(I) A factual programme that mixes narration, interviews, music and sound effects
(II) Listeners call the studio and speak on air
(III) A single speaker presents a subject to the listener
(IV) A story told through dialogue, music and sound effects
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: In a phone-in listeners call the studio (II). A radio feature is factual and mixes many elements (I). A radio drama tells a story through dialogue and effects (IV), and a radio talk has one speaker (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps phone-in and feature. (C) swaps feature and drama. (D) swaps drama and talk.
Key point: Radio formats differ in how many voices they use and whether they are factual.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: A model shaped like a spiral
questions.question: Frank Dance's model, which shows communication as growing and building on what came before, is shaped like a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Helix
Why: Dance's helical model (1967) shows communication as a spiral (helix) that keeps widening, since each exchange builds on earlier ones.
Why not the others: (A) describes linear models like Lasswell's. (B) describes the Osgood–Schramm model. (D) is the shape of the inverted pyramid in news writing, not a model of communication.
Key point: The helical model sees communication as a continuous, growing process.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Publishing news for undisclosed money
questions.question: News or analysis that appears in a paper in return for money, without telling readers that it was paid for, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Paid news
Why: Paid news is content passed off as news when it has been paid for, and readers are not told. The Press Council of India has called it a serious ethical lapse.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are paid content that is labelled as such. (B) is material that an organisation sends to the media for free.
Key point: The hidden payment is what makes paid news unethical.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Newspapers of the nineteenth and early twentieth century
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about newspapers in India:
(A) Samachar Darpan, started at Serampore in 1818, was a Bengali paper.
(B) Kesari was edited by Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
(C) Young India was edited by Mahatma Gandhi.
(D) Amrita Bazar Patrika became an English paper overnight to escape the Vernacular Press Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B), (C) and (D)
Why: All four are correct. Samachar Darpan (1818) was published in Bengali by the Serampore missionaries. Tilak edited the Marathi paper Kesari, and Gandhi edited Young India. In 1878 Amrita Bazar Patrika switched to English overnight, because the Vernacular Press Act applied only to papers in Indian languages.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) each leave out a correct statement.
Key point: The Indian-language and nationalist press played a large part in the freedom struggle.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: Parallel cinema films in order of release
questions.question:
Arrange the following films in the order of their release:
(A) Ardh Satya
(B) Bhuvan Shome
(C) Aakrosh
(D) Ankur
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (D), (C), (A)
Why: Mrinal Sen's Bhuvan Shome came out in 1969 and Shyam Benegal's Ankur in 1974. Govind Nihalani's Aakrosh followed in 1980 and his Ardh Satya in 1983.
Why not the others: (A) puts 1980 before 1974. (B) puts Ankur before Bhuvan Shome. (C) puts 1983 before 1980.
Key point: Bhuvan Shome is often taken as the start of the new wave of parallel cinema in Hindi.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: What FM stands for
questions.question: In radio broadcasting, FM stands for:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Frequency Modulation
Why: FM (Frequency Modulation) varies the frequency of the carrier wave to carry sound. It gives clearer sound than AM over a shorter range.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not the terms used.
Key point: AM varies amplitude; FM varies frequency.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Communication to a large scattered audience
questions.question: Communication through newspapers, radio and television to a large audience spread over a wide area is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mass communication
Why: Mass communication uses a medium to reach a large, scattered and mixed audience at the same time.
Why not the others: (B) is within a small group that can talk face to face. (C) is between two people. (D) takes place within one person's mind.
Key point: Mass communication needs a technical medium between sender and audience.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.sub_topic: Where to report cyber crime online
questions.question: In India, citizens can report cyber crime online on the national portal ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) cybercrime.gov.in
Why: The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, cybercrime.gov.in, lets citizens file complaints about online crime.
Why not the others: (B) is for RTI requests. (C) is the site of the Digital India programme. (D) is for citizens' participation in government.
Key point: Cyber crime can be reported on the portal or on the helpline.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: Film genres and their marks
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Genre)
(A) Biopic
(B) Thriller
(C) Horror
(D) Film noir

List-II (Feature)
(I) Dark, shadowy crime stories with morally unclear characters
(II) Aims to frighten the audience
(III) The life story of a real person
(IV) Builds suspense and tension
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: A biopic tells the life of a real person (III). A thriller builds suspense (IV). Horror aims to frighten (II), and film noir tells dark, shadowy crime stories (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps biopic and thriller. (B) swaps thriller and horror. (D) swaps horror and film noir.
Key point: A genre is recognised by its shared themes, settings and style.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: A copy-editing mark that cancels a change
questions.question: When a sub-editor wants a crossed-out word restored, they write the proofreading mark "____", meaning "let it stand".
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) stet
Why: "Stet" is Latin for "let it stand". It tells the printer to ignore a correction and keep the original text.
Why not the others: (A) means delete. (C) means set in capital letters. (D) means transpose, that is, swap two letters or words.
Key point: Copy editors use standard marks so that everyone reads them the same way.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Communication for development
questions.question: The use of communication to spread better farming methods, health practices and literacy in order to improve people's lives is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Development communication
Why: Development communication uses the media to bring social and economic change, for example campaigns on farming, health and education.
Why not the others: (A) concerns parties, elections and government. (C) is a company's communication with its public. (D) takes place within one person.
Key point: Krishi Darshan and SITE are early Indian examples of development communication.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Doordarshan becomes separate
questions.question: Doordarshan was separated from All India Radio and made a separate department in ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1976
Why: Doordarshan was separated from AIR on 1 April 1976.
Why not the others: (A) is when TV began in Delhi. (B) is when a daily TV service began. (C) is when a second TV centre opened in Bombay.
Key point: Television in India began as a part of All India Radio.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: The page that carries the paper's own view
questions.question: The article in which a newspaper states its own opinion on an issue is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) An editorial
Why: An editorial gives the newspaper's own view and is usually written by senior editors.
Why not the others: (A) is a longer human-interest story. (B) gives facts without the paper's opinion. (C) is a report of a person's death and life.
Key point: News and opinion are kept on separate pages.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: Microphones and the studio
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) A cardioid microphone picks up sound equally from all directions.
(B) A bidirectional microphone picks up sound from the front and the back.
(C) Ribbon microphones are delicate and are easily damaged by wind.
(D) Studio walls are treated with sound-absorbing material to cut down echo.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: (B), (C) and (D) are correct. A bidirectional microphone has a figure-of-eight pattern. Ribbon microphones are fragile. Acoustic treatment absorbs sound so that it does not bounce around the studio.
Why not the others: (A) is false. A cardioid microphone picks up mainly from the front in a heart-shaped pattern; an omnidirectional one picks up from all sides. Options (A) and (D) include (A), and (C) leaves out (C).
Key point: The pick-up pattern decides where a microphone hears from.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.sub_topic: A platform for short posts
questions.question: A platform on which users share very short posts and follow others' updates in real time is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Microblogging site
Why: Microblogging platforms such as X (formerly Twitter) carry short posts that followers see at once.
Why not the others: (A) is for careers and work contacts, like LinkedIn. (B) hosts videos, like YouTube. (D) carries long posts, like WordPress.
Key point: Social media platforms are grouped by the kind of content they carry.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: The father of Indian cinema
questions.question: Who is known as the father of Indian cinema?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Dadasaheb Phalke
Why: Dadasaheb Phalke made Raja Harishchandra (1913), the first full-length Indian feature film.
Why not the others: (A) made Pather Panchali (1955). (C) made Alam Ara (1931), the first Indian talkie. (D) was a later director and producer.
Key point: India's highest film award is named after Phalke.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Kind of advertisement that lists facts and figures
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Millet Foods, a farmer-producer company from Karnataka, is launching "Ragi Crunch", a baked ragi snack for school and college students. Its marketing head, Farah, meets an advertising agency and hands over a two-page document. It sets out the aim of the launch, the target audience (13–22 year olds in five cities), the budget of ₹40 lakh and the key message: "a tasty snack that is good for you".

The agency's first print advertisement shows the pack with a simple table: 8 g of fibre, 3 g of protein and no added sugar in every 30 g, a price of ₹20, and a list of stores. The agency then decides how the budget will be split between FM radio spots in the morning, posters on city buses and at bus stops, and short videos on Instagram, and in which weeks each will run.

Two months later, a rival brand releases an advertisement that says, "Our snack has twice the fibre of Ragi Crunch." Farah's team checks the rival's pack and finds the claim is true.

Question: The first print advertisement for Ragi Crunch, with its nutrition table, price and store list, is best described as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Informational advertising
Why: The advertisement gives the buyer facts about the product: what it contains, what it costs and where to buy it. This is informational advertising.
Why not the others: (A) promotes the image of a company, not one product. (C) promotes a banned product through another item with the same brand name. (D) is paid for jointly, for example by a maker and a retailer.
Key point: Informational advertising suits a new product that buyers know little about.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: The document a client gives an agency
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Millet Foods, a farmer-producer company from Karnataka, is launching "Ragi Crunch", a baked ragi snack for school and college students. Its marketing head, Farah, meets an advertising agency and hands over a two-page document. It sets out the aim of the launch, the target audience (13–22 year olds in five cities), the budget of ₹40 lakh and the key message: "a tasty snack that is good for you".

The agency's first print advertisement shows the pack with a simple table: 8 g of fibre, 3 g of protein and no added sugar in every 30 g, a price of ₹20, and a list of stores. The agency then decides how the budget will be split between FM radio spots in the morning, posters on city buses and at bus stops, and short videos on Instagram, and in which weeks each will run.

Two months later, a rival brand releases an advertisement that says, "Our snack has twice the fibre of Ragi Crunch." Farah's team checks the rival's pack and finds the claim is true.

Question: The two-page document Farah hands to the agency, setting out the aim, audience, budget and key message, is called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Client brief
Why: A client brief is the client's written statement of what the campaign must achieve, for whom, with what budget and with what message. The agency builds its creative work and media plan on it.
Why not the others: (A) is a set of drawings of the shots in a film or advertisement. (B) is the agency's later plan of when each advertisement appears. (C) is a set of material handed to journalists.
Key point: The brief is the starting point of the advertising process.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Form of advertising on buses and bus stops
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Millet Foods, a farmer-producer company from Karnataka, is launching "Ragi Crunch", a baked ragi snack for school and college students. Its marketing head, Farah, meets an advertising agency and hands over a two-page document. It sets out the aim of the launch, the target audience (13–22 year olds in five cities), the budget of ₹40 lakh and the key message: "a tasty snack that is good for you".

The agency's first print advertisement shows the pack with a simple table: 8 g of fibre, 3 g of protein and no added sugar in every 30 g, a price of ₹20, and a list of stores. The agency then decides how the budget will be split between FM radio spots in the morning, posters on city buses and at bus stops, and short videos on Instagram, and in which weeks each will run.

Two months later, a rival brand releases an advertisement that says, "Our snack has twice the fibre of Ragi Crunch." Farah's team checks the rival's pack and finds the claim is true.

Question: The posters on city buses and at bus stops are an example of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Transit advertising
Why: Transit advertising is placed on vehicles of public transport and at stops and stations, where commuters see it every day.
Why not the others: (B) is displayed in the shop where the product is sold. (C) is the small text advertisements grouped by category in a newspaper. (D) is posted to people's homes.
Key point: Transit advertising is a kind of outdoor advertising that moves with the audience.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Splitting a budget between media and weeks
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Millet Foods, a farmer-producer company from Karnataka, is launching "Ragi Crunch", a baked ragi snack for school and college students. Its marketing head, Farah, meets an advertising agency and hands over a two-page document. It sets out the aim of the launch, the target audience (13–22 year olds in five cities), the budget of ₹40 lakh and the key message: "a tasty snack that is good for you".

The agency's first print advertisement shows the pack with a simple table: 8 g of fibre, 3 g of protein and no added sugar in every 30 g, a price of ₹20, and a list of stores. The agency then decides how the budget will be split between FM radio spots in the morning, posters on city buses and at bus stops, and short videos on Instagram, and in which weeks each will run.

Two months later, a rival brand releases an advertisement that says, "Our snack has twice the fibre of Ragi Crunch." Farah's team checks the rival's pack and finds the claim is true.

Question: The agency's decision on how to divide the budget between radio, bus posters and Instagram, and when each will run, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Media planning
Why: Media planning means choosing which media will carry the advertisements, how much of the budget each gets, and the timing and frequency of the spots.
Why not the others: (A) is writing the words of the advertisement. (B) is dividing buyers into groups, which the brief has already done. (D) is the place a brand aims to hold in buyers' minds.
Key point: A media plan aims to reach the target audience at the lowest cost.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Judging the rival's comparison
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Millet Foods, a farmer-producer company from Karnataka, is launching "Ragi Crunch", a baked ragi snack for school and college students. Its marketing head, Farah, meets an advertising agency and hands over a two-page document. It sets out the aim of the launch, the target audience (13–22 year olds in five cities), the budget of ₹40 lakh and the key message: "a tasty snack that is good for you".

The agency's first print advertisement shows the pack with a simple table: 8 g of fibre, 3 g of protein and no added sugar in every 30 g, a price of ₹20, and a list of stores. The agency then decides how the budget will be split between FM radio spots in the morning, posters on city buses and at bus stops, and short videos on Instagram, and in which weeks each will run.

Two months later, a rival brand releases an advertisement that says, "Our snack has twice the fibre of Ragi Crunch." Farah's team checks the rival's pack and finds the claim is true.

Question: Which statement best describes the rival brand's advertisement?
options: A) It is covert advertising, as Ragi Crunch is named
B) It is banned, since no brand may name a rival
C) It is surrogate advertising for a banned product
D) It is comparative advertising, allowed if it is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It is comparative advertising, allowed if it is true
Why: The rival compares its product directly with a named competitor, so it is comparative advertising. Under the ASCI code such advertising is permitted when the claim can be proved and does not unfairly run down the other product. Farah's team found the claim true.
Why not the others: (A) Covert advertising hides the brand inside content; here the comparison is open. (B) Naming a rival is not banned in itself. (C) Nothing in the case is a banned product.
Key point: A comparison must be factual and fair, not disparaging.
